cards.front: What makes the primitive types primitive?
cards.back: They are built into the language — not objects, with no methods and no new
cards.extra: The eight of them (byte short int long float double char boolean) are keywords. Everything else you store is an object or a reference to one.

cards.front: How do you tell a primitive type from an object type in Java code?
cards.back: Primitives are lowercase keywords; object types start with a capital letter
cards.extra: int x = 5; versus String name = "Susan";. Convention, not syntax — but it holds for every class in the standard library.

cards.front: What does the dot in name.toUpperCase() actually do?
cards.back: It reaches into the object and gives you its members — methods and fields
cards.extra: The IDE lists them after you type the dot. Everything an object can do is behind that dot.

cards.front: How do you define a method that takes a parameter?
cards.back: public static void name(Type param) followed by a body in braces
cards.extra: The parameter is a local variable inside the method. public static just makes it callable from main without an object.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::02 Attributes and Methods

cards.back: It creates an object — allocates it and runs a constructor
cards.extra: Animal a = new Animal(); is the general shape: declare, allocate, assign the reference.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: How does the video define a class?
cards.back: A Java file that helps you make objects
cards.extra: Each class represents one kind of object with its own fields and methods. That is the whole of object-oriented programming at this level.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.back: Brings a class from a library into your file so you can name it
cards.extra: import java.util.ArrayList; — without it the compiler does not know the short name. The IDE offers the import when you hover a red type.
Without the type argument you get a raw list and every element comes back as Object. The angle brackets are the element type.

cards.front: How does an if / else if / else chain decide what runs?
cards.back: Exactly one branch — the first condition that is true, otherwise the else
cards.extra: The conditions are tested in order and stop at the first match. Order matters when conditions overlap.

cards.front: What does nesting a for loop inside another multiply?
cards.back: The number of executions — 8 outer iterations × 8 inner = 64
cards.extra: The inner loop runs completely for each outer iteration, which is why nested loops get expensive fast.

cards.front: What does ++ do in a loop?
cards.back: Adds one to the variable: a++ is a = a + 1
cards.extra: A while loop needs something inside to move the condition toward false, or it never ends.

cards.front: Why does the while loop in the video stop at 49?
cards.back: The condition a < 50 is false once a reaches 50, so the body never runs for 50
cards.extra: The condition is checked before each pass; when it fails the loop exits and control moves on.

cards.front: What does a try/catch block express?
cards.back: "Something may go wrong here" — the catch body runs if an exception is thrown
cards.extra: An exception means the normal path was interrupted. The catch receives the exception object describing what failed.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.back: It is the entry point — the JVM starts executing there
cards.extra: Nothing else in the file runs on its own. Methods are only executed when something calls them, starting from main.

cards.front: What is an API, in the video's terms?
cards.back: A published set of methods you can call from your own program
cards.extra: You add the provider's jar to the build path, import its classes, and call its methods — that is all "using an API" means at this level.
